identity.industry: Electronics Manufacturing Services (EMS) & Integrated Component Solutions

summary.oneLiner: Syrma delivered a landmark FY26 with 27% revenue growth and 270bps margin expansion to 11.3%, driven by high-margin ODM and export mix, while transitioning to a net cash position of INR467cr. Guidance for FY27 remains robust at 35% revenue growth and >10% margins, underpinned by a INR600cr order book and upcoming PCB capacity commissioning, though management guides conservatively on margins due to geopolitical raw material volatility.
summary.business: Syrma SGS Technology is an ESDM / electronics contract manufacturer serving over 350 customers across 35+ countries, offering PCB assembly, box-build integration, RFID solutions, high-frequency magnetic components and electro-mechanical assemblies as an end-to-end engineering and contract-manufacturing partner. Its operating model spans Automotive & EV, Consumer Electronics, Healthcare & MedTech, Industrial Systems, IT, Railways and a newly established Defence & Maritime division, with design-led ODM work now 17% of revenue and exports above 25% of consolidated revenue. The MD&A company overview cites 17 domestic manufacturing plants, an international facility in Stuttgart, Germany and R&D centres in Chennai, Pune, Bengaluru and Stuttgart; the BRSR, prepared on a standalone basis, separately reports 14 national plants and 8 national offices plus 1 international plant and 2 international offices.

Contract manufacturing / EMS: Printed Circuit Board Assembly (PCBA) - multi-layer circuit board engineering and assembly
Box-build integration - system-level assembly, mechanical housing integration and functional testing
Components and solutions: RFID solutions - high-frequency tags, inlays and software-integrated tracking systems
High-frequency magnetic components - custom magnetic coils, transformers and chokes
New offerings: EV powertrain and charging electronics - battery management systems (BMS), motor controllers, charging-interface sub-assemblies
Project pipeline: Integrated bare-board PCB manufacturing - HDI boards, copper-clad laminates and flexible circuits (Naidupeta, Andhra Pradesh, under construction)

currentContext.expansion: FY26 is described as a period of operational consolidation and strategic expansion, in which the business entered new growth segments through targeted acquisitions and partnerships, added domestic capacity and strengthened data security across production lines. The flagship project is an integrated bare-board PCB greenfield facility at Naidupeta, Andhra Pradesh - a ₹1,600 crores plant approved under the ECMS that will produce HDI boards, copper-clad laminates and flexible circuits, with civil works targeted for completion in the second quarter and trial production between December 2026 and early 2027; it is described as a major backward-integration step to cut reliance on imported bare boards and improve consolidated margins, addressing India's ~USD 6.3 billion bare-board PCB market which relies on imports for roughly 90% of supply, and running on state fiscal incentives and ECMS approvals. Civil works had commenced during the year. Inorganically, the Company acquired a 60% stake in Elcome Integrated Systems, a maritime and naval engineering specialist with nearly five decades of operating history, forming the operational foundation for the newly established Defence & Maritime division; and entered a joint venture with Italian electronics designer Elemaster, forming Syrma SGS Elemaster Private Limited, which operates out of a dedicated facility in Bommasandra, Bengaluru focused on high-reliability railway, medical and industrial electronics. The Company also became among the first manufacturers in India to secure TISAX certification for automotive data protection, clearing it for secure international electronic-component programmes. The stated existing footprint is 17 domestic manufacturing plants, an international facility in Stuttgart, Germany, and R&D centres in Chennai, Pune, Bengaluru and Stuttgart.
currentContext.mdna: Indian EMS structural growth: total Indian electronics production expanded roughly six-fold from ₹1.9 lakh crores in FY15 to ₹11.3 lakh crores in FY25 (17% CAGR FY2020-21 to FY2024-25), with MeitY projecting the broader ecosystem can reach USD 500 billion in production value by FY2030-31|The Indian EMS market (third-party manufacturing and design layer) was roughly USD 40-45 billion in FY2024-25, about 5-6% of global output, and is on course to approach USD 150 billion by FY2029-30 at upwards of 25% a year, close to four times the global pace; automotive, industrial, medical, defence and railway electronics scale fastest and hold the margin upside|Domestic consumption depth - rising incomes, lower durable prices under GST 2.0 and deeper smart-hardware penetration; India's EV registrations reached 25 lakh units in FY2025-26 (up 24.6%) with electric passenger-vehicle volumes up 86% to ~2.19 lakh units, lifting electronic-component value per vehicle|Export tailwinds - electronics was India's fastest-growing export category, USD 22.2 billion in H1 (up 42%) and USD 31 billion in the first eight months (up 38%), on track to become the country's second-largest export; India's share of global electronics exports rose from 0.6% in 2021 to 1.1% in 2024|Supply-chain diversification - exploratory sourcing reviews have firmed into multi-year procurement mandates with OEMs contracting secondary production outside China, with India a principal beneficiary|Vertical migration to higher-margin segments - naval electronics, aerospace sub-assemblies, advanced MedTech and railway signalling now draw sustained order flow from public-sector outlays and international sourcing, lifting operating margins|From assembly to ODM platforms - owning design, schematics and component selection deepens customer stickiness and margin durability, aided by India hosting the R&D of close to 80% of the world's semiconductor-design companies|Policy stack: PLI (cumulative production ~₹9.34 lakh crore, exports ₹5.12 lakh crores, ₹13,759 crores of capex by September 2025, tenure completing March 2026), ECMS (notified April 2025 targeting multi-layer PCBs, connectors, passives and advanced modules; outlay raised from ₹22,919 crores to ₹40,000 crore in the FY27 Union Budget), ISM/ISM 2.0, and Make in India / Electronics Manufacturing Clusters widening infrastructure across Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Karnataka; policy is pivoting from headline capacity toward domestic value addition targeted at roughly 38% by 2030|Automotive electronics content - rising electronic content, ADAS and fleet-tech features sustain automotive PCBA demand independent of powertrain-adoption speed; supported by PM E-DRIVE (extended for electric two-wheelers to July 2026 and three-wheelers to March 2028) and the ₹25,938 crores Auto and Auto-Component PLI|Industrial electronics - the global market was ~USD 211.4 billion in CY2025 heading to ~USD 412 billion by 2035 (6.9% CAGR); India's industrial automation sector was USD 17.28 billion in CY2025 heading to USD 38.02 billion by 2031 (14.05% CAGR), with low-to-medium volumes and strict thermal/vibration tolerances matching the engineering strengths of diversified Indian contract manufacturers|Industrial demand levers named: renewable energy and infrastructure build-out (rugged inverters, variable-speed drives, automated switchgear), industrial retrofitting with wireless sensors and cloud-connected cards, control-system electrification from mechanical controls to micro-controlled boards, and high-barrier engineering localisation clearing validation thresholds for railway, marine and aviation supply orders; capital commitments announced in 2024-25 crossed USD 50 billion across new semiconductor, appliance and automotive-component facilities|Agentic AI is pulling hardware demand beyond standard data centres into industrial, automotive and consumer endpoints|Lower US tariff lines (now at 10%) improve the financial returns of the Company's export-focused manufacturing lines|Stated OUTLOOK: a stable regulatory framework, improved US trade relations and a domestic demand base large enough to underwrite economies of scale lend the Indian EMS industry an encouraging medium-term outlook; the next phase will turn less on footprint growth than on the climb into component fabrication, full-stack design, semiconductor packaging and specialised verticals - an organisational-capability shift more than a capacity one|Margin/mix headwinds management flags: heavy import reliance on bare-board PCBs (~90%), capacitors and connectors squeezes margins until ECMS units come online; high energy intensity in fabrication, testing and assembly; exchange-rate swings and high ocean-freight rates|Most business verticals maintained a resilient order pipeline, with the Automotive, Consumer, and Industrial segments securing substantial momentum in order bookings

risks.note: Consumer remains ~30% of the portfolio - a share management describes as a deliberate cap on a 'lower-margin consumer business'. The mix shift out of consumer is the stated engine of margin expansion, so the residual consumer block is both a margin drag and a concentration exposure; excluding consumer, the core business grew 38% versus 27% consolidated.

risks.risk: Dependence on imported bare-board PCBs and other components
risks.note: The Company itself frames the Naidupeta project as 'a major backward-integration step to cut reliance on imported bare boards and improve consolidated margins', in a ~USD 6.3 billion Indian bare-board PCB market that relies on imports for roughly 90% of supply. Until the greenfield produces, input cost and supply continuity sit outside the Company's control.

risks.risk: Execution and ramp risk on the ₹1,600 crores Naidupeta greenfield
risks.note: A single large capital project carries a dated schedule - civil works completion targeted in the second quarter and trial production between December 2026 and early 2027 - and is a new product layer (HDI boards, copper-clad laminates, flexible circuits) rather than an extension of existing PCBA lines. Management notes returns were earned 'ahead of the main capital deployment for the bare-board PCB facility', so the capital is still to be spent.

risks.risk: Data security and customer data-governance compliance in automotive programmes
risks.note: Access to European premium automotive brands is gated on data-governance compliance; the Company had to secure TISAX certification 'satisfying the data-governance requirements of European premium automotive brands' to be cleared for secure international electronic-component programmes. FY26 work explicitly included strengthening data security across production lines.

risks.risk: Workforce, human-rights and labour-practice exposure across a large and partly contract workforce
risks.note: The employee base exceeded 10,000 as of 31 March 2026 across plants, R&D centres and offices in India and Germany, and the BRSR grievance framework explicitly covers contract workers and risks of forced/bonded labour, child labour, trafficking, sexual harassment, discrimination, unsafe conditions and wage theft. A failure here is a customer-audit and reputational risk in an export-facing B2B business, not only a compliance one.

risks.risk: Occupational health and safety in engineering and manufacturing operations
risks.note: The Company runs a structured incident regime covering near misses, first-aid cases, medical treatment cases and lost-time injuries, with engineering controls, machine guarding, PPE monitoring, ergonomic review, contractor safety management and permit-to-work - an acknowledgement that shopfloor injury risk is live and continuously managed rather than eliminated.

risks.risk: Breadth of enterprise risk overseen by a single Board committee
risks.note: Management states a structured enterprise risk management framework covering strategic, operational, financial, compliance and reputational risks, overseen by the Risk Management Committee of the Board and reviewed periodically against changes in the external operating environment. The routed text names the framework and its scope but does not enumerate the individual risks the Committee is tracking.

FY26 added an acquired maritime/naval business (Elcome, 60%) and a new joint-venture entity (Syrma SGS Elemaster) alongside new facilities; the human-resources commentary attributes part of the headcount step-up to 'the Elcome consolidation'. Absorbing a separately-run, higher-margin business into the Company's systems and controls is a live execution item.

one-line thesis: Syrma delivered a landmark FY26 with 27% revenue growth and 270bps margin expansion to 11.3%, driven by high-margin ODM and export mix, while transitioning to a net cash position of INR467cr. Guidance for FY27 remains robust at 35% revenue growth and >10% margins, underpinned by a INR600cr order book and upcoming PCB capacity commissioning, though management guides conservatively on margins due to geopolitical raw material volatility.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR1,477cr (Q4, +56% YoY), INR4,857cr (FY26, +27% YoY); EBITDA: INR174cr (Q4, 11.9% margin), INR545cr Operating (FY26, 11.3% margin, +270bps YoY); PAT: INR119cr (Q4, +67% YoY), INR346cr (FY26, +87% YoY, 7.1% margin); Order Book: INR600cr (as of Mar '26); Net Debt: Net Cash INR467cr (vs Net Debt INR264cr in FY25). One-offs: Reported EBITDA INR582cr includes Elcome contribution; Operating EBITDA excludes it. Accounting: Rating upgraded to AA.
guidance: Revenue Growth: ~35% for FY27; Margin: 10.5%-11.0% Operating EBITDA (conservative vs 12% current run-rate); Order Inflow: Continuous replenishment expected to sustain 35% growth; Capex/Commissioning: INR350-400cr in FY27 (INR250cr PCB + INR100-150cr organic); PCB commissioning expected end-FY27/start-FY28.
order book & pipeline: INR600cr total visibility; Mix: Auto 29%, Consumer 30%, Industrial 24%, Healthcare 5%, IT & Railways 11%. Management notes book is dynamic with short-duration orders (3-6 months) requiring constant replenishment to hit 35% growth target.
segment / subsidiary detail: IT & Railways: +182% YoY (Q4), +74% YoY (FY26), driven by laptops/motherboards/memory; Automotive: +39% YoY (domestic led, exports emerging); Healthcare (MedTech): +36% YoY, nearly 100% ODM mix, targeting INR500cr+ next year; Industrial: +30% YoY; Exports: +41% YoY to INR1,200cr+; ODM: +80% YoY to INR825cr (17% of revenue).
growth verticals / optionality: PCB Vertical: INR800cr capex plan (Phase 1 INR400cr) for multilayer/HDI/Flex PCB and CCL, commissioning FY28, adding incremental growth beyond organic 35%; Renewables: Pivoted from Ksolare acquisition to greenfield inverter manufacturing; Global Share Gain: Targeting wallet share increase from global Tier-1 customers; Addressable Market: Global EMS >$600bn, company at ~$500mn revenue.
margins & cost dynamics: Gross Margin improved 300bps to 25.6%; Operating Margin 11.3% (FY26) vs 8.6% (FY25). Cost Headwinds: Rising base metal prices, Middle East logistics disruption. Mitigation: Contractual pass-through mechanisms (with lag), better buying power, operational leverage. Guidance capped at 10.5-11% to buffer volatility despite 12% recent run-rate.
capex / expansion: FY26 Actual: INR140cr. FY27 Plan: INR350-400cr total (INR250cr for PCB Phase 1, INR100-150cr organic). Medium Term: Additional INR800cr for CCL/HDI/Flex PCB (FY28-FY30). Funding: Mix of internal accruals, debt, JV partner equity (25% for PCB), and government subsidies (expected 50-60% of PCB capex recouped over time).
capital allocation: Shifted from Net Debt INR264cr to Net Cash INR467cr (Cash INR820cr, Debt INR353cr); Debt/Equity 0.1x; ROCE 16.9% (20.1% goodwill-adjusted); Dropped Ksolare acquisition due to unfulfilled conditions; Focus on organic capex and selective M&A; Working Capital Days reduced from 69 to 63 (58 ex-Elcome).
risks & watch-items: Geopolitical supply chain disruptions (Middle East, shipping routes); Raw material inflation (base metals) with delayed pass-through; Competitive intensity from large conglomerates (e.g., L&T) entering EMS; Execution risk on PCB commissioning and subsidy realization; Customer concentration (Top 5 = 34%).
management quality / tone: Highly confident yet prudently conservative; Emphasizes 'quality of growth' (wallet share gains) over sheer volume; Transparent on margin guidance caution due to macro volatility; Strong focus on working capital discipline and cash generation.
non-obvious takeaways: MedTech segment is almost entirely ODM-driven, acting as a hidden margin engine; PCB subsidies create a 'circular' funding model reducing net cash outflow; Management explicitly willing to sacrifice top-line growth to protect working capital cycles; IT/Railways growth is lumpy but structural, not just cyclical.

hero.oneLiner: Syrma delivered a landmark FY26 with 27% revenue growth and 270bps margin expansion to 11.3%, driven by high-margin ODM and export mix, while transitioning to a net cash position of INR467cr. Guidance for FY27 remains robust at 35% revenue growth and >10% margins, underpinned by a INR600cr order book and upcoming PCB capacity commissioning, though management guides conservatively on margins due to geopolitical raw material volatility.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Syrma SGS Technology is an ESDM / electronics contract manufacturer serving over 350 customers across 35+ countries, offering PCB assembly, box-build integration, RFID solutions, high-frequency magnetic components and electro-mechanical assemblies as an end-to-end engineering and contract-manufacturing partner. Its operating model spans Automotive & EV, Consumer Electronics, Healthcare & MedTech, Industrial Systems, IT, Railways and a newly established Defence & Maritime division, with design-led ODM work now 17% of revenue and exports above 25% of consolidated revenue. The MD&A company overview cites 17 domestic manufacturing plants, an international facility in Stuttgart, Germany and R&D centres in Chennai, Pune, Bengaluru and Stuttgart; the BRSR, prepared on a standalone basis, separately reports 14 national plants and 8 national offices plus 1 international plant and 2 international offices.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian EMS structural growth: total Indian electronics production expanded roughly six-fold from ₹1.9 lakh crores in FY15 to ₹11.3 lakh crores in FY25 (17% CAGR FY2020-21 to FY2024-25), with MeitY projecting the broader ecosystem can reach USD 500 billion in production value by FY2030-31
- The Indian EMS market (third-party manufacturing and design layer) was roughly USD 40-45 billion in FY2024-25, about 5-6% of global output, and is on course to approach USD 150 billion by FY2029-30 at upwards of 25% a year, close to four times the global pace; automotive, industrial, medical, defence and railway electronics scale fastest and hold the margin upside
- Domestic consumption depth - rising incomes, lower durable prices under GST 2.0 and deeper smart-hardware penetration; India's EV registrations reached 25 lakh units in FY2025-26 (up 24.6%) with electric passenger-vehicle volumes up 86% to ~2.19 lakh units, lifting electronic-component value per vehicle
- Export tailwinds - electronics was India's fastest-growing export category, USD 22.2 billion in H1 (up 42%) and USD 31 billion in the first eight months (up 38%), on track to become the country's second-largest export; India's share of global electronics exports rose from 0.6% in 2021 to 1.1% in 2024
- Supply-chain diversification - exploratory sourcing reviews have firmed into multi-year procurement mandates with OEMs contracting secondary production outside China, with India a principal beneficiary
- Vertical migration to higher-margin segments - naval electronics, aerospace sub-assemblies, advanced MedTech and railway signalling now draw sustained order flow from public-sector outlays and international sourcing, lifting operating margins
- From assembly to ODM platforms - owning design, schematics and component selection deepens customer stickiness and margin durability, aided by India hosting the R&D of close to 80% of the world's semiconductor-design companies
- Policy stack: PLI (cumulative production ~₹9.34 lakh crore, exports ₹5.12 lakh crores, ₹13,759 crores of capex by September 2025, tenure completing March 2026), ECMS (notified April 2025 targeting multi-layer PCBs, connectors, passives and advanced modules; outlay raised from ₹22,919 crores to ₹40,000 crore in the FY27 Union Budget), ISM/ISM 2.0, and Make in India / Electronics Manufacturing Clusters widening infrastructure across Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Karnataka; policy is pivoting from headline capacity toward domestic value addition targeted at roughly 38% by 2030
- Automotive electronics content - rising electronic content, ADAS and fleet-tech features sustain automotive PCBA demand independent of powertrain-adoption speed; supported by PM E-DRIVE (extended for electric two-wheelers to July 2026 and three-wheelers to March 2028) and the ₹25,938 crores Auto and Auto-Component PLI
- Industrial electronics - the global market was ~USD 211.4 billion in CY2025 heading to ~USD 412 billion by 2035 (6.9% CAGR); India's industrial automation sector was USD 17.28 billion in CY2025 heading to USD 38.02 billion by 2031 (14.05% CAGR), with low-to-medium volumes and strict thermal/vibration tolerances matching the engineering strengths of diversified Indian contract manufacturers
- Industrial demand levers named: renewable energy and infrastructure build-out (rugged inverters, variable-speed drives, automated switchgear), industrial retrofitting with wireless sensors and cloud-connected cards, control-system electrification from mechanical controls to micro-controlled boards, and high-barrier engineering localisation clearing validation thresholds for railway, marine and aviation supply orders; capital commitments announced in 2024-25 crossed USD 50 billion across new semiconductor, appliance and automotive-component facilities
- Agentic AI is pulling hardware demand beyond standard data centres into industrial, automotive and consumer endpoints
- Lower US tariff lines (now at 10%) improve the financial returns of the Company's export-focused manufacturing lines
- Stated OUTLOOK: a stable regulatory framework, improved US trade relations and a domestic demand base large enough to underwrite economies of scale lend the Indian EMS industry an encouraging medium-term outlook; the next phase will turn less on footprint growth than on the climb into component fabrication, full-stack design, semiconductor packaging and specialised verticals - an organisational-capability shift more than a capacity one
- Margin/mix headwinds management flags: heavy import reliance on bare-board PCBs (~90%), capacitors and connectors squeezes margins until ECMS units come online; high energy intensity in fabrication, testing and assembly; exchange-rate swings and high ocean-freight rates
- Most business verticals maintained a resilient order pipeline, with the Automotive, Consumer, and Industrial segments securing substantial momentum in order bookings

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY26 is described as a period of operational consolidation and strategic expansion, in which the business entered new growth segments through targeted acquisitions and partnerships, added domestic capacity and strengthened data security across production lines. The flagship project is an integrated bare-board PCB greenfield facility at Naidupeta, Andhra Pradesh - a ₹1,600 crores plant approved under the ECMS that will produce HDI boards, copper-clad laminates and flexible circuits, with civil works targeted for completion in the second quarter and trial production between December 2026 and early 2027; it is described as a major backward-integration step to cut reliance on imported bare boards and improve consolidated margins, addressing India's ~USD 6.3 billion bare-board PCB market which relies on imports for roughly 90% of supply, and running on state fiscal incentives and ECMS approvals. Civil works had commenced during the year. Inorganically, the Company acquired a 60% stake in Elcome Integrated Systems, a maritime and naval engineering specialist with nearly five decades of operating history, forming the operational foundation for the newly established Defence & Maritime division; and entered a joint venture with Italian electronics designer Elemaster, forming Syrma SGS Elemaster Private Limited, which operates out of a dedicated facility in Bommasandra, Bengaluru focused on high-reliability railway, medical and industrial electronics. The Company also became among the first manufacturers in India to secure TISAX certification for automotive data protection, clearing it for secure international electronic-component programmes. The stated existing footprint is 17 domestic manufacturing plants, an international facility in Stuttgart, Germany, and R&D centres in Chennai, Pune, Bengaluru and Stuttgart.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Over four decades of operating experience in high-mix, flexible-volume manufacturing for high-margin, fast-growing industrial sectors
- Breadth of customer base and reach - over 350 customers across 35+ countries, serving 18 Indian states and 39 countries
- Design-led capability rather than build-to-print assembly: ODM revenue grew 80% to Rs 825 crore and rose from 12% to 17% of revenue, described as a primary driver of margin expansion
- Established European credibility - close to three decades serving European customers and an own engineering facility in Stuttgart since 2008, described as operating credibility that cannot be replicated overnight
- TISAX automotive data-protection certification clears the Company for secure international electronic-component programmes with European premium automotive brands
- Backward integration into bare-board PCB via the Naidupeta greenfield, addressing a ~USD 6.3 billion Indian market that relies on imports for roughly 90% of supply
- Engineering depth - more than 195 engineers across four R&D centres; employee base above 10,000 as of 31 March 2026
- Long-term credit rating upgraded from AA- to AA during the year
- Sites located inside major domestic electronics clusters, with an export footprint above 25% of revenue
- Shift toward longer-cycle, stickier work through naval/maritime entry, joint ventures and the first multi-year, multi-product long-term framework contract
